title: Teaching at Amherst, mentors Joe Dixon and Billy Mitchell, school jazz bands
summary: He teaches part time and recalls Long Island mentors; they discuss the loss of the big-band apprenticeship and school jazz bands whose students do not listen.

bands.name: Nassau County Youth and Euphonic Jazz Orchestra

story.theme_name: Teaching jazz: schools, students and advice to the young
story.community_name: Becoming a teacher: jazz in schools and conservatories

blocks.x: I mean you do a lot of educational work?

I do a lot of education but I don’t have any full time teaching position. I’m presently the adjunct processor of jazz saxophone at Amherst College. And I have a handful of students every semester. But for me, I really love jazz ed — I love jazz teaching and being in that world. I had a lot of incredible mentors when I was a teenager growing up. I had — when I was growing up on Long Island there was an alto saxophone-clarinet-flute player named Joe Dixon who was a — he played with Bunny Berrigan and Artie Shaw, and you know, he was very active in the swing era, and he had a jazz ensemble of teenagers in Nassau County on Long Island called the Nassau County Youth and Euphonic Jazz Orchestra. And he became a really strong mentor. And when I grew up there were some amazing saxophone players on Long Island: Billy Mitchell was from Detroit, he played with Thad Jones, he was really a powerful force, and I had a chance to play with him a lot and get my butt kicked from him as well. So that’s — it’s important © Hamilton College Jazz Archive -4-

for young musicians to have that experience, and because of the demise of touring big bands, you know the apprenticeship system is kind of disappearing. So young musicians coming out of college are forced to kind of really create their own situation and create their own scene.
That’s also interesting, that almost every junior high and high school in the country has a jazz band now, a swing band. But not that many of these students actually listen to the music.

Yeah, that’s a problem. And the music is not easy to find in a lot of cases. It’s still very much an underground music in the sense that it’s not prevalent on television, it’s not easy to find on the radio unless it’s a college station that has jazz programming, it’s not mainstream in our society. So unless you have a band teacher who really is into the music and brings in records and exposes the students to the music, it just becomes just another ensemble for them to play the music without really even understanding the language and how it’s really meant to be played. But the fact that those ensembles exist is really a great sign and the fact that there is support from the administration and support from the community to keep those ensembles going, I think that’s huge. Because the kids need some kind of exposure and the younger the better.
